4026.dq: High tones are assigned to the rightmost accent in a word, and also to the leftmost mora (the marked case) or first mora after the leftmost foot (the unmarked case) of a word. This High tone is then moved to the head of the foot it is in. All moras dominated by or located between High tones within a word are pronounced on a High pitch.

Some words are accentless and take High on the final mora (fn. 9).

4026.tone: Source (p. 115) calls Nakijin 'a pitch accent language with an iambic foot structure. Stress plays no role in the phonology'; abstract p. 111: 'a pitch accent language with no phonemic stress'. The accent is lexical (penultimate vs. ultimate mora, plus accentless words) and is realised as a High-tone span whose left edge is set by foot structure (first mora after the leftmost foot) and whose right edge is the rightmost accent. Quantity-sensitive iambic feet exist (iambic lengthening, foot-initial aspiration) but carry no stress and are independent of accent position. Corroborating saved files (not the primary source): Ogawa 2012 NINJAL Project Review 7 p. 41 gives three surface noun types (A high from 1st/2nd mora, B high from 3rd–5th mora, C initial-mora high with obligatory fall; mora is the unit; rising kernel); Curry 2004 §2.1.4 pp. 34–37 gives Martin's A/B/C types and says both register and locus of the fall are needed, with no mention of stress; Nagano-Madsen 2014 pp. 51–52 classes Nakijin as the rising-kernel accent type distinct from Shuri's fixed 2nd-mora falling kernel and from accentless Irabu; Lawrence 2017 p. 1 says Nakijin is unusual among Ryukyuan in having an accent in addition to tone.

4030.prule: No word-stress rule is stated; word prosody is a grammatically predictable tone system. Verb roots are underlyingly toneless; each tense assigns one 'melodic H' to the 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th mora of the (macro)stem (mora-counting, not syllable-counting), and in tonally inflected tenses that H spreads rightward onto all non-phrase-final moras (i.e. to the penult); the Hortatory Imperative has no melodic H. 4030.tone: First-hand source (Marlo, Mwita & Paster 2015; co-author Mwita is a native speaker) calls Kuria a 'predictable' Bantu tone language with two surface tones (H, L) and no lexical tonal contrast in verb roots; the melodic H is assigned by mora count (mu1-mu4) and spreads to the penult but never onto the phrase-final mora. The only occurrence of 'stress' about Kuria is fn 17 (pp. 262-263), a reviewer's typological remark that no stress system targets the fourth syllable (Heinz 2009), used against a metrical (foot-based) analysis of the mu4 melody; Sect. 3.2 'A metrical approach' discusses foot parses as an analysis of tone placement, not stress. Philippson 1991 (Sect. 6.2.2.1 'Le cas du kuria', pp. 270-272, and Annexe p. 501) reanalyses the same facts as a 'langue a accent' whose accents 'sont realises comme des tons H', with the accent on one of the first four moras of the maximal verb stem and, for nominals, normally on the stem-initial mora: a pitch-accent relabelling of the H-tone system; he lists no intensity/length culmination for Kuria and Kuria is absent from his p. 484 lists of penultimate-culmination languages. Either way the verdict is tone or pitch accent; no source reached mentions penultimate lengthening. One reached source does mention stress: Whiteley 1955 (PhD thesis, SOAS; fieldwork at Tarime, Butimbaru dialect, Nov. 1952-Feb. 1954 and Jan.-Feb. 1955, five named informants), Ch. 3 'The Tone of the Verbal', sec. 1, p. 103 (PDF p. 108): after stating that Kuria has 'two level contrastive tones; high and low' (p. 102) and that 'the significance of grammatical tone is considerable' (p. 103), he writes 'As might be expected in a language where pitch is significant, stress is characteristic rather than distinctive. In verbals there is a stress on the radical, and on V(owel)1 and V(owel)3 in poly-syllabic radicals: in radicals of shape -C- a stress occurs on the syllable immediately preceding the radical.' This is an impressionistic auditory remark (no procedure or measurement stated for stress, no examples marked for stress), it concerns verbals only, it treats stress as non-distinctive in a pitch language, and no later first-hand source (Marlo et al. 2015, Mwita 2012, Philippson 1991) repeats it; it does not move the verdict from tone. For tone the entry now rests on Marlo et al. 2015, quoted in the tone block.

Bwamu laa is described as a three-level register tone language (phonological tones H, M, B; lexical and grammatical tone) whose tone-bearing unit is the syllable, which may carry more than one tone (attested word melodies H, M, B, HM, HB, MH, MB, BH, BM, MHM, BHB, HMH, HMB, HBM, p. 51). The only remark on native word accent is the author's explicit statement that whether bwamu laa has an accent at all is unknown and still to be studied ('l’accent du bwamu laa (s’il y en a)', p. 95); no stress position, weight condition or lexical-stress claim appears anywhere in the thesis.

4046.idn: bwamu laa (láá láá), the dialect of the departments of Bagassi, Pa and Boni; informants from Banou (dép. Bagassi) and Boni; data: data from two native-speaker participants (Ernest Tindo of Banou, Adolphe Homboué of Boni) at an SIL tone workshop in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, 22 February - 11 March 2011…
4046.tone: Three phonological tone levels H, M, B (p. 49), confirmed against Bolli, Flik & Bivando 1981 and Manessy 1961:127 ('trois tons ponctuels: haut, moyen, bas', with raised/lowered realisations 'dans certaines conditions'). A fourth 'suprahaut' tone claimed by Yé 1981 for the Bagassi dialect is rejected (pp. 47-49) as a phonetic raising under emphatic or repeated pronunciation ('on accentue plus et un ton haut est prononcé plus haut que normal', p. 47) or a HB fall on a light syllable. Syllable, not mora, is the UPT/TBU (p. 51). Tone association is left-to-right, one-to-one, with spreading and grammatical tone processes; tonal pronouns ('pronoms toniques') are tone-stable at phrase start. In French loans the French final word accent is reproduced as a high tone in 43 of 48 items (pp. 90-91, §2.10.2.1) and the French accented/unaccented opposition is rendered as H/B (pp. 97-100); this is tone assignment to loans, not a native stress rule. On native stress/accent the source is explicitly agnostic (p. 95, 's’il y en a'), citing Naden 1989:155 that Gur 'pitch and accentual phenomena' remain unresolved.
